one_line: Hands-on test of Llama Coder, a free open-source prompt-to-app builder on Together AI. It improved after switching to Llama 3.3 but still fell short of Cursor, Windsurf, Bolt.new and v0.
summary: The host tests Llama Coder, a free open-source prompt-to-app builder found on X that runs on Together AI and uses Llama models. The first task-manager build had non-working category and add-task features, and repeated fix prompts did not resolve them. Pasting a ChatGPT-generated prompt did not help either. Switching to Llama 3.3 and enabling the ShadCN UI toggle produced a working app, after the host pasted a runtime error back into the prompt box. The host then used a Publish button to get a shareable link and showed the GitHub repo's local-run steps. On a calculator prompt, Llama 3.3 gave a basic app, Qwen 2.5 Coder gave a better interface, and Gemma 2 was weak. The host concludes it is not a strong free alternative to Cursor, Windsurf, Bolt.new or v0, and that it could not build full-stack apps initially. The evidence is one prompt per model with no quantitative comparison.

key_ideas.idea: Llama Coder is a free open-source prompt-to-app builder on Together AI, with a side panel for the generated app and a separate changes prompt box.
key_ideas.detail: Found on X. The host prompts for a task-organizer app; the first build is basic and its category dropdown does not add categories.

key_ideas.idea: Repeated follow-up fix prompts did not repair broken features on the default model.
key_ideas.detail: Add-task still failed after several fix requests, including a ChatGPT-written structured prompt. The generated code errored each time.

key_ideas.idea: Switching models was the change that made the app work, not prompt quality.
key_ideas.detail: After switching to Llama 3.3 and turning on the ShadCN UI toggle, the app started. The host then pasted the runtime error back into the prompt box and the app became functional.

key_ideas.idea: The host attributes the improvement to Llama 3.3 and makes unsourced claims about its benchmarks and cost.
key_ideas.detail: He says it outperforms Gemini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4 Omni on coding, math and reasoning, and is far cheaper. He gives no numbers or sources.

key_ideas.idea: Structure was not delivered: the requested dashboard with separate category pages became a filter UI.
key_ideas.detail: The host calls the filter workaround acceptable because it works. Tasks added in one round did not appear until a fix was requested.

key_ideas.idea: Published apps get a shareable link, and the repo can be run locally with a Together API key.
key_ideas.detail: The Publish button copies a link to the clipboard. A GitHub button links the open-source repo, which the host describes as an open-source Claude-artifact-style app built with Llama.

key_ideas.idea: Model choice matters: on a calculator prompt Qwen 2.5 Coder beat Llama 3.3 and Gemma 2 on UI quality.
key_ideas.detail: Llama 3.3 gave a basic app, Qwen 2.5 Coder gave a clearly better interface, and Gemma 2 was not good. Each model got one run.

key_ideas.idea: Verdict: not a strong free alternative to Cursor, Windsurf, Bolt.new or v0, and it did not handle full-stack apps at first.
key_ideas.detail: The UI also needed a lot more work even with ShadCN. The host suggests trying other tools if you need a stronger builder.

techniques.name: Run Llama Coder locally from the GitHub repo
techniques.how: 1) Click the GitHub button at the top right and copy the git clone command. 2) Clone the repo. 3) Create an env file holding your Together API key (sign up via the link provided on the project's page). 4) Run npm install. 5) Run npm dev (as shown in the video) to start the app.
techniques.when: When you want to try the open-source builder yourself or keep it off the hosted service.

techniques.name: Paste runtime errors back into the change prompt box
techniques.how: Copy the error shown in the generated app and paste it into the changes prompt box, then ask for a fix.
techniques.when: When the generated app throws an error. In this test this worked once the model was switched, but not on the default model.

techniques.name: Switch the generation model from the dropdown
techniques.how: Pick Llama 3.3 instead of the default model. For UI-heavy prompts, try Qwen 2.5 Coder (it produced the best interface in the calculator test).
techniques.when: When a model keeps failing on the same prompt. Switching was the fix that worked here.

techniques.name: Enable the ShadCN UI toggle
techniques.how: Turn on the ShadCN UI toggle before generating so the app uses ShadCN pre-built components.
techniques.when: When you want generated front-ends built on a component library rather than raw HTML.

techniques.name: Publish and share the generated app
techniques.how: Click Publish app. The app is deployed and its link is copied to the clipboard.
techniques.when: When you want a quick hosted preview of the generated app.

techniques.name: Use the built-in placeholder prompt for a calculator
techniques.how: The project provides a placeholder calculator prompt. The host used it verbatim to compare models.
techniques.when: For a repeatable, same-prompt comparison across models.

numbers.claim: Speaker says Llama 3.3 is about 25 times cheaper than GPT-4 Omni (unsourced claim).
Speaker says Llama 3.3 outperforms Gemini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and GPT-4 Omni on coding, math and reasoning (no benchmark numbers given).
Runs: about 3 generation rounds before the task-add flow worked. One calculator run per model, three models compared.

hot_takes: Llama 3.3 is the only change that visibly fixed the app. The host credits the model, but he changed the prompt and the error handling too, so the cause is not isolated.
Verdict is negative: not comparable to Cursor, Windsurf, Bolt.new or v0, and the UI needs much more work even with ShadCN.
Title asks whether it is worth it, but the evidence is one anecdotal run per model. Benchmark and cost claims about Llama 3.3 are unsourced.
Quality capped at 2: thin, single-prompt evidence and a clickbait-style 'Is it WORTH it?' framing, although the trial is honest about its failures.

relevance.why: It is a browser-based builder, not a Claude Code CLI harness, and it covers no checkpointing, approvals or credentials.
